title: Heaps and RID Lookups
description: On a heap, a nonclustered seek does a RID Lookup per row; a covering index eliminates the lookup. Why it matters: heaps (tables with no clustered index) are more common than people expect in legacy schemas, and this RID-lookup cost is a frequent, under-diagnosed drag on performance.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine a filing cabinet where papers are just tossed in wherever there happens to be room, with no particular order at all — but you keep a separate index card catalog that tells you, for any topic, exactly which folder number holds the paper you want. That catalog is useful, but to actually retrieve the paper, you still have to go dig out that specific folder from wherever it physically sits in the unsorted cabinet. This lesson is about a table with no primary organizing structure at all — called a heap — and about the extra step needed to fetch a full row from it even when an index tells you exactly which row you want.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** In SQL Server, if a table has a clustered index (most commonly built on the primary key), the table's actual data rows are physically stored in that index's order — the index *is* the table, organized. But if a table has no clustered index at all, it's called a "heap": the rows just sit in storage in whatever order they happened to be inserted, with no meaningful physical ordering. A heap can still have nonclustered indexes built on it (indexes that point at specific rows by column value), but this lesson is about what those indexes actually have to point *at*, in the absence of a clustered index to organize the fetch.

**Why this happens in real databases.** Heaps are more common than people expect in legacy schemas and quick-and-dirty table designs — a table created without explicitly designating a primary key as a clustered index, or one where a clustered index was later dropped for some reason, silently becomes a heap without anyone necessarily realizing the implications. It still works fine for basic reads and writes; the difference only shows up in exactly how a nonclustered index has to fetch full rows.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** On a table *with* a clustered index, a nonclustered index stores, for each entry, the clustering key (the primary key value, typically) as its "pointer" back to the full row. So looking up extra columns not present in the nonclustered index means using that clustering key to do a "key lookup" — essentially, a second seek into the clustered index using the same efficient B-tree seek mechanism as the first lookup. On a heap, there's no clustered index to seek into at all, so the nonclustered index instead stores a physical address — literally, "file number, page number, slot number on that page" — called a RID (Row Identifier), as its pointer. Fetching the rest of the row is then a "RID lookup": go directly to that specific physical location and read whatever's sitting there.

This sounds like it should actually be *faster* than a key lookup, since it's a direct physical address rather than a B-tree seek — and for a single lookup, it roughly is. But the RID pointer has a serious downside: it's fragile. If a row on a heap gets updated in a way that makes it too big to fit back in its original physical slot, SQL Server can't just leave it — it moves the row to a new location and leaves behind a "forwarding pointer" at the old spot, so anything still holding the old RID gets redirected to the new location, adding an extra hop to the lookup. Over time, as a heap accumulates enough of these forwarded rows from ordinary updates, RID lookups increasingly involve chasing forwarding pointers around, quietly degrading what should be a single direct hit into an extra, invisible detour.

More fundamentally though, this lesson is about the same core issue seen elsewhere: whether it's a key lookup (on a table with a clustered index) or a RID lookup (on a heap), needing to go fetch additional row data one extra time *per matching row*, on top of the initial index seek, adds up fast as the number of matches grows — the exact same "seek plus N extra lookups" cost curve, whether those lookups happen to be into a B-tree or straight to a physical address.

**Why this matters in production.** Heaps are an easy thing to end up with by accident — simply not adding a clustered index (or explicitly choosing "no clustered index" in a design tool) is enough — and their behavior under indexed lookups is subtly different and, over time, worse than a properly clustered table, due to the forwarding-pointer degradation that comes with heap updates. The practical fix demonstrated in this lesson is the same core idea as covering a non-covering index elsewhere in this course: make the nonclustered index "covering" by including every column the query needs directly in the index (via `INCLUDE`), so there's no RID lookup needed at all — the index alone has everything the query asked for, eliminating both the extra lookup cost and any risk of chasing forwarding pointers on an aging heap.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below runs a query against a heap table using a nonclustered index that doesn't cover every needed column, and shows you the RID Lookup operator fetching the rest of each row's data by physical address. After making the index covering with `INCLUDE`, re-run the query and watch the RID Lookup disappear entirely — the index alone now has everything the query needs, with no separate trip back to the heap's physical storage required at all, regardless of how fragmented that heap may have become from ordinary updates.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** It's worth being able to recognize a heap in the first place — in SQL Server Management Studio or any metadata query, a table with no clustered index shows up in `sys.indexes` with no row where `index_id = 1` (clustered indexes always occupy `index_id` 1; a heap simply has no row there at all). Converting a heap to a proper clustered table, by adding a clustered index (usually on the primary key), is often a bigger overall performance win than trying to work around the heap's RID-lookup and forwarding-pointer quirks — it's worth considering as the first option whenever a legacy table turns out to be a heap unintentionally.

## Scenario
`Orders` is a **heap** — a table with *no clustered index*. A screen runs `SELECT CustomerId, OrderDate, Total, Status FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 42`. There is a nonclustered index on `CustomerId`, yet the query still does far more I/O than the ~40 rows it returns.

## Why it's slow
A heap stores rows in no particular order and identifies each by a physical **RID** (file:page:slot). The nonclustered index on `CustomerId` can **seek** to the matching index rows, but it only holds `CustomerId` (plus the RID). To fetch `OrderDate`, `Total`, and `Status` the engine must follow each RID back into the heap — a **RID Lookup**, driven by a **Nested Loops** operator, once per matching row.

## What to look for
- In the plan: an **Index Seek** feeding a **Nested Loops** that does a **RID Lookup** into `Orders`.
- In `STATISTICS IO`: logical reads well above the row count — one lookup per row.

## The concept
This is the heap version of a Key Lookup. Eliminate it the same way: make the index **covering** with `INCLUDE (OrderDate, Total, Status)` so the seek returns every needed column and never touches the heap. (Adding a clustered index is the other common fix — it changes lookups from RID Lookups to Key Lookups, but covering the query removes the lookup entirely.)
startingQuery: SELECT CustomerId, OrderDate, Total, Status FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 42;
hints: The seek finds the rows, but which operator fetches the other columns? Look for a Nested Loops / RID Lookup on Orders.
IX_Orders_CustomerId holds only CustomerId — it can't supply OrderDate, Total, or Status without a lookup into the heap.
Create a covering index: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Cust_Cov ON Orders(CustomerId) INCLUDE (OrderDate, Total, Status);
